analysis.title: What Next For US Politics And Equities?
key_insights: A Democratic Congress is a modest constraint on Trump, not control. Democrats lack the 2/3 Senate vote (they will have 56) needed to override a veto or remove him, so his tax and spending laws stand.
Equity returns going forward are expected to be tied more to policy, including the Fed, than to rerating of tech sector valuations.

Democrats are not expected to shrink the budget deficit, only to change what it finances. The size of the majority reduces the sway of the party's extremist wing, since red states and districts delivered it with centrist candidates.

Congress has limited tools to affect the war with Iran. The 2006 Democratic Congress sent Bush a $124bn Iraq funding bill with a withdrawal timetable and he vetoed it, and Trump has found workarounds to the War Powers Act.
The first items for the new Congress are the debt limit and FY27 appropriations including defence. Ukraine, tariffs and ICE will be priorities, with investigations but no impeachment.

Bipartisan pressure is expected on export controls for advanced technology sales to China and on Russia sanctions. AI regulation is also expected to get bipartisan support, since AI power plants were a major election issue and TX, OH and GA flipped governorships to Democrats.

Historically the S&P 500 generally rallies after mid-terms, but the party that wins does not determine direction. In four of the six mid-terms since 2002 the market kept the direction it had before the election. 2018 fell 9% from election day to year-end because of Fed tightening, not the House result.
The VIX shows no consistent trend into or out of mid-terms, averaging 21.9 pre-election and 19.5 post. At about 20 it sits near the 16.92 median since Sep 2002, so the author calls it a non-event.

Sector correlations point to a sector correction rather than a broad bear market. In Q4 to date, non-tech sectors show more negative correlation with the S&P 500 and tech. Without GOOG and NVDA the S&P rose 0.8% in October.

The S&P 500 is called fairly valued. A forward P/E of 20.9 is a 4.78% earnings yield, implying a 15-year doubling, against 13 years for nominal GDP growth (5.69% 10-year average) and 14 years for the 10Y zero-coupon at 4.91%. The 10Y is not yet cheap enough to pull money out of stocks.

September JOLTS showed the hiring rate rising in information, lifting the private-sector total. The author sees this as year one of a recovery after a non-recession recession in 2025, with profits leading hiring.
The economy improves in 2027 and the equity market will reflect it. Base inflation moves higher as growth continues and the Fed lags.

sector_views.rationale: Current weakness is described as a sector correction rather than a broad bear market. Excluding GOOG and NVDA the S&P rose 0.8% in October.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Implies the price doubles in 15 years, close to nominal GDP growth, so the market is called fairly valued.
Implies GDP doubles in 13 years, similar to the equity market's implied pace.
Money doubles in 14 years, about the same as the S&P, so the 10Y is not yet cheap enough to pull money from stocks.
Close to the 16.92 median since Sep 2002 and treated as a non-event.

macro_indicators.reading: Hiring rate rose in information and lifted the private sector total
macro_indicators.interpretation: Hiring is starting to catch up with profits, in line with year one of a recovery.
Growth continues while the Fed lags, so inflation worsens and policy yields lag.

risk_factors: Trump's policies, including geopolitical events, are the main driver of equity returns and are hard to constrain.
Debt limit and FY27 appropriations must be resolved first.
Inflation rises as growth continues and the Fed lags.
Hiring could reverse in 2027 (the author refers to his earlier note on the risk of reversion).
A concentrated tech sector decline, with the S&P down 1.4% in the sample period.
charts_described: Chart 1 plots the VIX around mid-term elections from 2002 to 2026 and shows no discernible trend, with the average at 21.9 pre-election and 19.5 post.

Chart 3 plots the y/y difference in hiring rate by sector from Jan 25 to Sep 26 for total private, information, manufacturing, FIRE and professional and business services.

VIX near 20 versus a median of 16.92 since Sep 2002, so not extraordinary.

geopolitical: Congress's limited ability to change the course of the war with Iran, with the Iraq War and War Powers Act as precedent

tension_points.bull_case: The equity market generally rallies after mid-terms, and markets like divided government as a constraint on activism.
tension_points.bear_case: The market tends to keep its pre-election direction, and with Trump the division may matter little. Policy, not rerating, is the main risk.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Fed tightening as in 2018, when the S&P fell 9% from election day to year-end despite Democratic House gains.

tension_points.theme: tech sector correction vs bear market
tension_points.bull_case: Increased negative correlations between non-tech sectors and the S&P show a sector correction, and the S&P rose 0.8% in October without GOOG and NVDA.
tension_points.bear_case: Sector correlations tend toward one in a bear market, which would signal a broader decline.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Sector correlations with the S&P 500 moving toward one.

theme_stances.key_argument: After the mid-terms the equity market typically strengthens into year-end, and the market is fairly valued against GDP and the 10Y.
theme_stances.evidence: equity market generally rallies after the mid-terms

theme_stances.theme: tech sector correction not bear market
theme_stances.key_argument: Increased negative correlations in Q4 vs Q3 show a sector correction rather than a broader bear market.
theme_stances.evidence: the current market is correcting a sector rather than shifting into a broader bear market

theme_stances.key_argument: Congress has few tools to counter Trump, so policy risk remains the main driver of returns.
theme_stances.evidence: Congress has few quivers, if any, to shoot down or counter his plans
